paras: The threatened lynching of John Miller took place at Havana, Mason County, Illinois, in mid-January 1881, when townspeople prepared to lynch Miller after his arrest on an accusation that he had killed a young child. Guards placed over him kept the crowd away, and no violence against him was reported. The case drew notice chiefly for the accusation itself, which the Canton Register called one of the most horrible in the history of crime.

According to the Canton Register, Miller lived with a woman whose child was about three, and while she was away he was accused of kicking and choking the child until it was dying. He then called a physician, saying the child had spasms; the physician left the house on the pretext of going to the drug store and called the city marshal, who arrested Miller. A wire brief dated the arrest to a Friday afternoon, apparently 14 January, and gave the child's age as four.

When news of the affair spread, the Register wrote, "the enraged citizens made preparations to lynch Miller," but the guards placed over him had kept the "would-be lynchers" at bay up to the time of writing. The paper did not say how many took part or where Miller was held.
No report of an inquest, indictment or trial of Miller was found, and no one was reported arrested for the threat against him.

The fullest account appeared in the Canton Register, an Illinois paper, on 21 January under the headline "A [Brutal] Murder." The Register treated the accusation as proven, calling Miller "a thing in human form" and "the fiend," and did not criticize the would-be lynchers. It nonetheless closed by demanding a lawful hanging, writing that "if Miller does not hang for it justice must indeed be dead in Mason county."

Elsewhere the story ran only as a one-sentence arrest item in the Delaware Daily Republican on 17 January and the Delaware State Journal on 20 January, neither of which mentioned a mob. None of these reports gave the race of Miller, the child or the crowd.

bases: Citizens of Havana made preparations to lynch a man in custody but guards kept them off, so this is a threatened lynching with no violence reported (A3).
No one was killed or injured: the 'would-be lynchers' were kept at bay by guards (A3); the crowd acted without authority on an accusation of child murder, but its size is not stated.
Miller's arrest is reported in a wire brief (A1, reprinted in A2) and in the Canton Register (A3), but only A3 reports the preparations to lynch him.

accounts.label: Wire brief
accounts.gist: John Miller was arrested at Havana on Friday afternoon for choking and kicking to death the four-year-old child of a woman who lived with him; nothing about a mob.

accounts.label: Canton Register (Illinois paper)
accounts.gist: A physician called to the house alerted the city marshal, who arrested Miller; when the news spread, enraged citizens prepared to lynch him, but guards had kept them at bay up to the time of writing.

framing.detail: The Canton Register's 'A [Brutal] Murder' presented the accusation as fact ('the fiend's brutality'), reported the guards holding off the 'would-be lynchers' without comment on them, and demanded that Miller hang lawfully.
Two Delaware papers ran a one-sentence arrest item in news summaries, with no mention of a mob.

conflicts.note: The Canton Register, an Illinois paper that named the county and gave the fuller story, is the more detailed source; the one-line wire brief may be less exact.

record_check.record: A farmer's boy threw a rope over the head of a man accused of murder and called for volunteers to lynch him. Officers arrived and took him to the county jail, where a strong guard restrained the excited crowd.
record_check.dossier: The rope, farmer's boy and county-jail details come from the tail of the Ottawa Free Trader's 'An Ohio Horror' about Robert Garnes at Plain City, Ohio, not from the Havana case; for Miller the papers report only that citizens prepared to lynch him and guards kept them at bay.
